papers.title: Clinical and biomarker predictors of α-synuclein seeding in cognitive impairment and motor parkinsonism.
papers.abstract: Dopamine transporter (DAT) imaging and α-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA) are biomarkers for Lewy body disease (LBD). We aimed to identify clinical and biomarker factors associated with SAA positivity in patients with cognitive impairment and frequent motor parkinsonism. Dual-phase DAT positron emission tomography (PET) scans, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) phosphorylated-tau/β-amyloid ratio (PTAR) measurement, and SAA were performed in 108 patients, including 99 with motor parkinsonism. Diagnoses, which were not mutually exclusive, included normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH, N = 60), Alzheimer's disease (AD, N = 53), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB, N = 43), vascular cognitive impairment (VCI, N = 23), progressive supranuclear palsy (N = 3), and semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (N = 1). We investigated clinical and biomarker factors associated with SAA positivity, including clinical diagnoses, clinical features, striatal DAT uptake, and log-transformed PTAR (LN-PTAR), and examined whether SAA positivity was associated with dopaminergic degeneration and regional perfusion measured by dual-phase DAT PET. SAA was positive in 50 patients (46.3%), including 30 of 43 (69.8%) with DLB and 47 of 99 (47.5%) with motor parkinsonism. Seven (14.0%) SAA-positive patients showed normal DAT uptake. Among clinical diagnoses, DLB and AD were associated with a higher likelihood of SAA positivity, whereas NPH and VCI were associated with a lower likelihood. Among clinical features, cognitive fluctuations and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder were independently associated with SAA positivity. Among biomarker measures, lower posterior putamen DAT uptake and a higher LN-PTAR were independently associated with SAA positivity. SAA positivity was associated with lower posterior putamen DAT uptake on delayed-phase DAT PET but not with perfusion changes on early-phase DAT P

papers.title: Dopaminergic state modulates shame and contextual emotional responses in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BackgroundShame is frequent in Parkinson's disease (PD) and negatively affects quality of life, yet its dopaminergic modulation remains unclear.MethodsWe investigated the effect of dopaminergic replacement therapy (DRT) on shame in 41 fluctuating PD patients using an experimental tailored shame induction task. At visit 1, participants were presented with 60 short written scenarios (neutral, non-PD-related shame, PD-related shame). A tailored selection of 12 scenarios (4 per category) was generated in three steps: (1) initial rating of all 60 scenarios on a shame/embarrassment visual analogue scale (VAS); (2) selection of the highest-rated scenarios for shame conditions and lowest-rated scenarios for neutral condition to account for individual emotional relevance; and (3) emotional rating of these scenarios on 10 VAS (fear, sadness, disgust, joy, self- and other-directed anger, shame, embarrassment, guilt, stress) to ensure specificity of shame/embarrassment responses. At visits 2 and 3, patients rated the 12 scenarios once ON- and once OFF-DRT (randomized crossover design) using the same 10 VAS.ResultsIn OFF-DRT state, shame ratings were lower than in ON-DRT for non-PD-related shame scenarios (Zratio = -2.53, p = 0.02), with a similar trend for PD-related shame scenarios (Zratio = -2.02, p = 0.06). Conversely, patients reported higher embarrassment (Zratio = 4.53, p < 0.001), stress (Zratio = 3.49, p < 0.001), and self-directed anger (Zratio = 3.99, p < 0.001) when evaluating scenarios rated as neutral in the ON-DRT state.ConclusionsIn OFF-DRT state, emotional responses showed altered contextual calibration, with reduced shame in shame-eliciting contexts and increased negative emotions in neutral situations. These findings suggest that dopaminergic state may modulate intensity and appraisal processes of emotions.

papers.title: Oral Microbiota Associated With Parkinson'S Disease: A Systematic Review.
papers.journal: Special care in dentistry : official publication of the American Association of Hospital Dentists, the Academy of Dentistry for the Handicapped, and the American Society for Geriatric Dentistry
papers.abstract: AIMS: To evaluate the available evidence on the association between oral microbiota composition and Parkinson's disease (PD), including its relationship with disease severity and clinical features. METHODS AND RESULTS: This systematic review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024560059) and conducted according to the PRISMA 2020 statement. Searches were performed in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, LILACS, Scopus, and SciELO. Observational studies evaluating the oral microbiota of adults with PD were included. Eleven studies, predominantly case-control, were analyzed, with 16S rRNA sequencing used in 90.9% of them. The genera most frequently associated with PD were Lactobacillus (45.45%), Prevotella (36.7%), and Streptococcus (36.7%). Most studies reported differences in beta diversity, indicating a distinct oral microbial profile in patients with PD. Higher Lactobacillus abundance and lower Neisseria abundance were associated with greater disease severity and poorer cognitive performance in some studies. According to the GRADE approach, the certainty of the evidence was very low. CONCLUSION: The available evidence suggests that PD is associated with alterations in oral microbiota composition. However, because the evidence is derived predominantly from observational studies, causal relationships cannot be established. Longitudinal studies using standardized microbiome methodologies are needed to validate these microbial signatures as candidate biomarkers.

papers.title: A novel oxidative-inflammatory biomarker for Parkinson's disease: clinical utility of the uric acid-to-albumin ratio.
papers.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Emerging evidence highlights the contribution of systemic inflammation and oxidative stress to the pathogenesis and progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). Accordingly, blood-based biomarkers that capture these processes are of increasing clinical interest. This study evaluated the association between PD and serum uric acid, serum albumin, and their integrated index-the uric acid-to-albumin ratio (UAR)-to determine their potential utility as biomarkers of systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, and disease progression. METHODS: A total of 153 patients with PD and 291 healthy controls were included. Serum uric acid, albumin, and UAR were measured through standardized biochemical assays. Group comparisons and multivariable logistic regression were performed to assess associations with PD, and analyses stratified by Hoehn and Yahr stage examined relationships with disease severity. RESULTS: Uric acid, albumin, and UAR levels were significantly lower in patients with PD compared with healthy controls (all p < 0.001). After adjustment for age, sex, hypertension, and diabetes, UAR remained independently associated with PD, with lower UAR corresponding to higher odds of disease (OR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.63-0.82, p < 0.001). Stratified analyses showed that UAR reductions were most prominent in early and middle PD stages, whereas advanced-stage values approximated those of controls. ROC analysis demonstrated moderate discriminative ability of UAR for PD overall (AUC = 0.630) and for early-to-middle stage disease (AUC = 0.620 and 0.644, respectively). CONCLUSION: UAR is significantly reduced in PD and associated with early-middle disease stages, supporting its potential as an accessible biomarker for PD monitoring, though larger longitudinal studies are needed for validation.

papers.title: The glymphatic-lymphatic axis: known pathways, open questions, and emerging roles in neurodegeneration.
papers.abstract: The discovery of the glymphatic system and meningeal lymphatic vessels has transformed our understanding of brain fluid homeostasis and central-peripheral communication, highlighting the critical role of cerebrospinal fluid in brain clearance. While substantial progress has been made in defining the structural components and physiological regulators of brain clearance, major uncertainties remain regarding (1) how these systems interact as an integrated physiological network, (2) how they fail in disease, and (3) whether they can be therapeutically manipulated. In this review, we first summarize the anatomical and physiological organization of the glymphatic-lymphatic axis, with particular emphasis on its regulatory mechanisms in light of rapid advances in this field. We then discuss how the glymphatic-lymphatic axis functionally integrates with peripheral immune and metabolic systems and describe how impairment of these clearance pathways is associated with the accumulation of pathological proteins, neuroinflammation, and vascular dysfunction and may contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Finally, we discuss emerging therapeutic strategies and biomarkers targeting the glymphatic-lymphatic axis. By redefining the central-peripheral crosstalk, the glymphatic-lymphatic axis provides a unifying framework for understanding brain clearance, neurodegeneration, and future therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: Deep brain stimulation for arm tremor: one-year blinded follow-up of a randomized trial.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To present the secondary endpoints at one-year blinded follow-up from our randomized controlled study, that compared the efficacy of DBS in the ventral-intermediate thalamic nucleus (VIM) with the posterior subthalamic area (PSA) three months each in crossover design, and showed significantly greater reduction of the Sum dominant arm tremor score (Fahn-Tolosa-Marin) during the PSA-DBS period. The outcomes at one year are now reported to verify target choice and sustained benefit with clinically optimized free programming. METHODS: Forty-five patients with isolated or combined arm action tremor received four-level DBS leads to reach both VIM (upper two levels) and PSA (lower two), and were randomized post-operatively to VIM-DBS month 1-3 followed by PSA-DBS month 4-6, or vice versa. Thereafter electrode choice was free as judged by best clinical outcome. Predefined secondary endpoints were the tremor score improvements from preoperative to the one-year follow-up for dominant and non-dominant arm, other body regions, total score, two patient-rated measures and adverse events. RESULTS: At the one-year follow-up, Sum dominant arm tremor scores had improved from median 24 at baseline to 4 (p<.001, n = 43), corresponding to median 79% improvement. All other secondary endpoints also improved significantly (p<.001). Median action tremor improvement was for Essential tremor(ET) 83%, for Parkinson´s disease(PD) and Dystonic tremor 100% and for Cerebellar tremor 55%. Over 90% of stimulated contacts were in PSA. INTERPRETATION: At one year, good and sustained tremor suppression from PSA-DBS was confirmed in ET, PD and Dystonic tremor. Suppression of Cerebellar tremor was more variable. TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT03156517, May 29, 2017.
